title: Love bade me welcome
hookLine: a guest who feels unworthy is welcomed anyway: sit and eat (Love III)
carry: so I did sit and eat
tomorrow: God gives people every gift but one. which one, and why?

cards: Invited to dinner, and the first instinct is to apologize: sorry I'm late, sorry I didn't bring anything, sorry, I can't have you back yet.
George Herbert, an English country priest, wrote that feeling into a poem: "Love bade me welcome: yet my soul drew back, Guilty of dust and sin."

teach.b: Love, in the poem, is God, and the guest keeps finding reasons to stay in the doorway. I'm not worthy to look at you. Love takes his hand: who made the eyes but I?
Then I've ruined them, he says; let my shame go where it deserves.
And know you not, says Love, who bore the blame? Then at least let me serve. No.
"You must sit down, says Love, and taste my meat: So I did sit and eat." That's the end. No speech.
Just a meal, and someone eating it. Taste is the whole argument.
The teaching is the Christian word grace: a welcome you don't earn and can't pay back. Herbert's guest can't host in return, and isn't asked to.

Readers hear the communion table in it, and Jesus' picture in Luke of a master who comes home and waits on his own servants: "he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them."
There's a story behind the book, too.
Izaak Walton, Herbert's early biographer, tells that Herbert, dying, sent his poems to a friend: publish them if they might help any dejected poor soul; if not, burn them.

teach.h: SO I DID SIT AND EAT.

how: Christians speak of grace as God's welcome that can't be earned, and churches gather at the communion table. Herbert's Love (III) is read in Anglican circles and beyond, and Vaughan Williams set it to music in his Five Mystical Songs.

games.q: what does “love bade me welcome” mean?
o: a wedding toast that welcomes the bride's whole family
an old greeting painted over the door of an English inn
Herbert's line: God's welcome to a guest who feels unworthy

games.q: the guest and the host: tap the pairs.
p: so I did sit and eat

s: in Herbert's poem, the guest earns his seat by serving
he offers to serve, and Love says no: you must sit down and taste my meat.
Herbert was a priest in a small English parish
a country priest; Izaak Walton wrote his life.
Herbert published his poems while he was alive
Walton tells that, dying, he sent them to a friend to publish or burn.

games.q: a new coworker keeps turning down the team's lunch invites because she "hasn't earned it yet." what fits Herbert's poem?
o: a welcome isn't wages; sometimes the answer is just to sit and eat.
she's right to wait until she has proven herself.
she should buy lunch for everyone first, then accept.
games.why: Love answers every excuse, refuses the offer to serve, and the guest simply sits and eats. that's grace.

practice: Take one bite of something, or one sip: bread, fruit, tea. Before you eat, notice any pull to earn it, rush it, or explain it. Then taste it slowly, all the way through, the way Herbert's guest finally did.

wordCard.voice: Love bade me welcome: the first line of Herbert's poem, where God invites a guest who keeps drawing back.

carryVoice: Your line: so I did sit and eat. In Herbert's poem, grace doesn't send a bill. That's eighteen of twenty-one.
